               COMMENTS OF THE OHIO ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL


       On behalf of the Ohio Environmental Council (“OEC”) an Ohio, state-wide,

not-for-profit organization committed to protecting the environment and health of all

Ohio communities through legal and policy advocacy, decision-maker accountability,

and civic engagement, we hereby provide the following comments regarding the study

agreement filed by PJM Interconnection in this proceeding.

       The October 13, 2026 filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Docket No.

ER27-126-000), regarding a Study Agreement in Furtherance of the State of Ohio’s

State Agreement Approach (SAA) Request, raises serious questions about the potential

for the shifting of project costs onto ratepayers; threatens to subvert regional grid

protections; undermines of the spirit and intent of PJM’s SAA mechanism; and

highlights growing concerns about the long-term viability of the proposed PORTS-Pike

Technology Campus and the infrastructure it demands.




                                                                                          1
 Cost-shifting onto ratepayers

       Given the structural financial risks associated with the project, FERC should

reject PJM’s request to use the SAA absent a clear and legally-binding cost-allocation

structure that ensures 100% of the transmission infrastructure project costs are posted

up front by the developer.

       Should the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus’ proposed 10-GW load enter the

PJM footprint, it would radically alter the region's supply-to-demand balance. Despite

developers plans to pair the data center campus with a 9.2-GW behind-the-meter gas

plant, the campus will operate 24/7/365. If that gas plant is down for maintenance at any

point, or if its full capacity doesn’t come online fast enough, this massive tech campus

will rely heavily on the regional grid for its energy needs. Demand of this scale could

tighten the overall capacity market, driving up the regional clearing price for electricity.

Even a slight increase in wholesale capacity costs across PJM’s territory could translate

into billions of dollars in aggregate rate hikes that are socialized across all captive retail

customers, entirely separate from the initial line-construction costs.

       While SB Energy (the developer) may pay for the immediate 765-kV lines

connecting to the Baku, Hanging Rock, and Gavin substations, the campus’ massive

power demands could trigger many secondary grid strains—such as overloaded

transformers and local voltage drops throughout the region. AEP Ohio could classify

fixes to these strains as "local grid reliability" or "supplemental" upgrades, rather than

direct project interconnections, and could fold those costs back into the general rate

base, raising the standard distribution rates for everyday utility customers across Ohio.




                                                                                                 2
 Systemic risks: speculative investment, extreme counterparty concentration

       It is also of grave concern that the developer, SB Energy, presently has zero

operating data centers and zero revenue from AI. The company incurred billions of

dollars in net losses in early 2026, largely due to speculative AI investments. In filing

documents for its since-delayed Initial Public Offering (IPO), SB Energy stated that it is

“substantially dependent” on the performance of OpenAI as both a tenant and equity

investor.

       In addition to OpenAI being signed on as the sole tenant for the PORTS project

and another proposed SB Energy datacenter in Texas, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is

also an early personal investor in SB Energy. Concurrently, SB Energy’s parent

company, the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank, has finalized a $64.6 billion cumulative

investment in OpenAI, and holds a 13% equity stake in the AI lab as of October 2026,

making SoftBank OpenAI's second-largest external shareholder, after Microsoft.

       Meanwhile, Nvidia has agreed to a staggering $105 billion financial guarantee to

backstop OpenAI’s lease, while OpenAI has committed to exclusively using Nvidia chips

at the site–Nvidia is expecting roughly $200 billion in chip sales for the project’s first

phase alone.

       SB Energy postponed its IPO in September as its sought-after valuation of $50

billion was met with skepticism from investors. Bankers have reportedly struggled to find

enough buyers of SB Energy stock within the company’s target price range. OpenAI is

also planning an IPO in 2027, delayed from its original 2026 target amid concerns about

AI safety as well as competitive threats from open-source models and the astronomical

capital expenditures required to sustain its business over the coming decades. The




                                                                                             3
 company forecasts nearly $280 billion in negative free cash flow through 2030, driven

by soaring spending on infrastructure and compute costs.

       The financial loop among the small and deeply interconnected network of

companies involved with the PORTS-Pike project creates an enclosed system of capital

and infrastructure commitments. Should any of these parties’ financial positions waver,

or if the broader AI market faces a structural downturn (which many experts warn is

likely), the entire project could collapse. A mid-project failure of this magnitude could

shift billions of dollars in infrastructure and grid stabilization costs onto PJM ratepayers,

and saddle Ohio with the massive public burden of an abandoned 10 GW hyperscale

datacenter on the site of a former federal uranium enrichment facility that has not been

fully remediated.



Unprecedented use of State Agreement Approach

       Using a special public-policy tool such as the State Agreement Approach (SAA)

to fast-track a hyperscale project on behalf of a highly speculative corporate entity with

no relevant operational track record presents extreme risks for ratepayers in the PJM

system, as well as for Ohio’s economy and energy future. Such an application of the

SAA is also unprecedented for PJM, and represents a major departure from the tool’s

intended purpose and historical use.

       Historically, the SAA has been used as a tool for states to achieve and pay for

environmental public policy objectives. The mechanism allows states to work with PJM

on transmission upgrades required to meet policy goals, and take on the costs of those

specific projects.The SAA has only been utilized twice in the past – both times by the




                                                                                                4
 New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to interconnect offshore wind. The proposed use of

the SAA for the PORTS-Pike project repurposes the tool purely to support a large-scale

commercial data center development, effectively leveraging an approach intended to aid

in the development of public infrastructure into a fast-track mechanism benefiting a

massive private tech campus with no clear public policy objective.

      The State Agreement Approach would establish a coordinated process to

evaluate the proposed data center expansion, related power generation and

transmission facilities as a single integrated project. This allows the PORTS-Pike

Technology Campus project to bypass PJM’s standard, "first-come, first-served"

interconnection queue, treating the campus as a state-driven public policy initiative

rather than a private commercial development.

      If FERC accepts this application of the SAA, it risks creating a dangerous

precedent, signaling to states that the SAA can be used to bypass standard

interconnection queues and fast-track private development projects under the guise of

“economic development” without clear policy objectives or public benefits.



November 3, 2026​ ​        ​      ​      ​      ​

Respectfully Submitted,
